bio.en: Manik Gupta led two of history's most successful consumer products - Google Maps as director of product and Uber as Chief Product Officer - and later joined Microsoft as a Corporate VP.
bio.zh: 马尼克·古普塔（Manik Gupta）曾领导史上最成功的两款消费级产品——作为产品总监领导 Google Maps，并担任 Uber 的首席产品官——后来以企业副总裁身份加入微软。

summary.en: Manik shares lessons on building consumer products, structuring product teams, and the difference between company-market fit and product-market fit. He reflects on what it was like to be CPO at Uber versus Google versus Microsoft. The episode also offers career advice for anyone aiming to become a CPO.

turns.zh: 我自己每天也使用Coda。它是我的写作和播客运营的核心。我用它进行初稿创作，组织内容日历，规划每期播客，以及许多其他用途。Coda为本期播客的听众提供首笔消费满1000美元的免费信用额度，只需访问coda.io/lenny即可。就是coda.io/lenny。（00:03:03）：马尼克，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: Thank you, Lenny. It's great to be here, man.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，莱尼。很高兴能来这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know if it's obvious, but I am quite honored to have you on this podcast. You've had such an illustrious career as a founder leading the Google Maps team, as CPO at Uber for, I believe, four years. Now you're kind of a fancy VP at Microsoft on consumer stuff. It's this incredible career and trajectory. My first question is, looking back at your career, what would you say is maybe the one or two main things that you did that helped you get to where you are today? For folks that are maybe earlier in the career, of what they should be focusing on.
turns.zh: 我不知道是否显而易见，但能邀请您参加这次播客，我深感荣幸。您作为谷歌地图团队创始人兼负责人的辉煌职业生涯，以及在优步担任首席产品官四年的经历，都令人赞叹。如今您在微软担任消费者业务副总裁，职业生涯可谓惊人之旅。我的第一个问题是，回顾您的职业生涯，您认为哪些关键举措助您走到了今天？对于处于职业生涯早期的人们而言，您认为他们应该重点关注哪些方面？

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: Yeah. Thanks, Lenny, for having me. I'm also a big fan of yours, by the way. I love your newsletter and it's been incredible to just see how you have also grown both the set of topics that you cover and this podcast. Just really a big fan, so again, thanks for having me.
turns.zh: 是啊。感谢您邀请我，伦尼。顺便说一句，我也是您的忠实粉丝。我很喜欢您的时事通讯，见证您拓展报道领域和播客内容的成长实在令人惊叹。真的非常欣赏您，感谢您的邀请。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Appreciate that.
turns.zh: 多谢夸奖。

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: Let me start by telling you a little bit about my philosophy of this. I'm maybe a little bit late to the party, but I recently read this book from Morgan Hausel on Psychology of Money. And I highly recommend your listeners read it if they get a chance. There's a chapter in there, he talks about luck and risk. What he says is, when you look at individuals and you think about, or you ask them, or you think about what they have done that have made them successful, we tend to put a greater amount of emphasis on effort and a little less emphasis on luck and risk. I think I strongly subscribe to that. The important thing when you look back is how much luck played a big part, and of course the risk that somebody took played a big part. (00:04:45): This is something that I've been thinking a lot about myself, which is what are some of the patterns of people who have had multiple careers and have gone through a journey where they've learned a lot and they've contributed and things like that? I think there are two patterns that stand out, both when I look at myself in terms of what I've been through, and also when I talk to a lot of my friends who have also gone on and done interesting things, and I wanted to cover both of that. The first one is really about people. It's about surrounding yourself with the best people you can find. (00:05:16): It was so funny. I was watching the Warriors game last night, and yeah Warriors, we won the NBA championship. That's great.
turns.zh:
首先，我想谈谈我对此的看法。可能我入行有点晚，但最近我读了摩根·豪塞尔的《金钱心理学》一书。强烈推荐听众有机会的话去读一读。书中有一章讲运气与风险。他指出，当我们观察成功人士时，往往更强调努力，而对运气和风险重视不足。我深有共鸣。回顾过往时，重要的是要认识到运气和冒险精神在成功中所起的关键作用。

（00:04:45）：这也是我自己一直在思考的问题——那些拥有多重职业生涯、历经磨难并有所建树的人，有哪些共同的模式？我总结出两个关键点：一是围绕最优秀的人才组建团队。（00:05:16）：太有趣了。昨晚我看了勇士队的比赛，勇士队赢得了NBA总冠军，真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Go Warriors.
turns.zh: 勇士队加油。

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: One of the reporters, I think she asked Steve Kerr, the coach, "What's the secret?" And he goes, "Well just hang around superstars." That's what he said and he just passed the mic over to somebody else and said, "Look, this is a team that's hanging around superstars." And that's exactly what it is. If you're create enough opportunities, especially early on in your career as you asked, around hanging around people who are doing interesting things and they're doing things which really are different, or they're doing things in a different manner and it's exciting, the right things will happen. (00:05:55): I was lucky in a way that I caught myself in that situation. I grew up in India and when I was 16 I got a scholarship to move to Singapore to do my high school and then my undergrad studies. It just turned out that during those days, Singapore... I mean it still is, but it was a melting pot for the best and brightest folks that you can get from all over the Asia diaspora if you will. Among my colleagues and my fellow students there were a bunch of really, really smart people, so I just learned a lot from them and that gave me a great start to just go on and do something interesting. Right out of college, I started my own company and I did that with two of my classmates. One of them happens to be one of my best friends whom I grew up with who also came on the same scholarship with me to Singapore. We were just part of that ecosystem and it gave me a lot of opportunities to try out different things in college and so on and so forth. (00:06:44): I think the main thing that I would say here for people who are early in career is just surround yourself with people who are really good at what they do. Learn from them. And by the way, play the long game. Once you find someone like that, stick to them. As long as they want to hang out with you, but just stick to them. Because you will go on to do multiple things over your career with the same set of people. And the shared trust and experience that you build with A plus people is just going to go a long way. Anyway, that's pattern number one. I think that has helped me a lot and I also see a lot of that in other folks whom I talk to. (00:07:19): Then the second pattern is... This is something I resonate a lot with personally, is I'm a strong technology optimist. There's always a lot of narrative these days around technology and maybe a little bit more pessimism, and I find that bizarre. I'm just such a strong technology advocate and optimist, because I feel technology's such a strong force for good. I grew up as an engineer myself, and I've always been attracted to projects where we can use technology to solve a real human need. I did that with my startup, I did that at Hewlett-Packard, I did that at Google and at Uber as well. The passion that you get if you're a strong advocate of technology and how it can really help, it just gets you to choose a set of things that you want to do at scale. (00:08:06): For instance, when I joined Google in India to work on Maps, it was all about helping millions of users, around Asia particularly, navigate their world. There wasn't a good solution like that, so how can you bring technology to really solve those problems? (00:08:21): I think those are the two patterns, Lenny. One is surrounding yourself with A plus people, and the second is just having very strong optimism and passion about technology. At least if I connect their dots looking backwards, those are the things that have really helped me and a bunch of other folks that I see in a similar situation. I'm hoping that folks early in their career thing through that.
turns.zh:
其中一位记者，我记得她问主教练史蒂夫·科尔：“秘诀是什么？”他回答：“嗯，就是和超级巨星待在一起。”他就这么说完，然后把麦克风递给别人，接着说：“看吧，这支球队就是和超级巨星待在一起的。”而这正是事实。只要你能创造足够多的机会——尤其是像你提到的职业生涯初期——去接触那些正在做有趣事的人，他们的做法确实与众不同，或是采用了令人兴奋的不同方式，正确的机遇就会降临。（00:05:55）：我算幸运的，因为我恰好身处这样的环境。我在印度长大，但16岁时获得奖学金前往新加坡完成高中和大学学业。当时的新加坡正如你所说，是一个汇聚了亚洲各地最优秀人才的熔炉。在校友和同学中，有许多极其聪明的人，我从他们身上学到了很多，这为我日后做有意义的事奠定了基础。大学一毕业，我就和两位同学创办了自己的公司，其中一位是我儿时的好友，也是和我同获奖学金来到新加坡的。我们深深融入了那个生态圈，这让我在校期间有机会尝试各种事物。（00:06:44）：对于职业生涯初期的人，我想说最重要的是：多和行业精英共处，向他们学习。顺便说一句，要有长远眼光。一旦找到这样的人，就紧紧抓住他们。只要他们愿意与你共事，就坚持下去。因为你职业生涯中的许多成就都会与同一批人共同创造。与顶尖人才建立的信任和积累的经验将带来深远影响。这就是第一条经验。我认为这对我帮助很大，从我接触的其他人身上也能看到类似的成功之道。（00:07:19）：第二条经验与我个人共鸣很深：我是个坚定的技术乐观主义者。如今关于技术的讨论多带有悲观色彩，我觉得这很奇怪。我始终是技术的忠实拥护者，因为技术本质上是推动社会进步的强大力量。我自己就是工程师出身，从小就被吸引到能用技术解决现实人类需求的项目中。我在初创公司、惠普、谷歌和优步都做过这样的事。作为技术的坚定支持者和信仰者，如果你对技术能带来改变充满热情，就会自然而然地选择一系列可以大规模推广的事业。（00:08:06）：比如，我加入谷歌印度团队负责地图项目时，核心目标是帮助亚洲数百万用户导航世界。当时并没有成熟的解决方案，所以如何用技术真正解决这些问题呢？（00:08:21）：这就是两条经验，莱尼。一是与顶尖人才共处；二是保持对技术的乐观和热情。至少从我回顾过往的经历来看，这两条经验确实对我和许多处境相似的人都带来了巨大助力。
我希望处于职业生涯初期的人们能认真考虑这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I bet there's a big overlap between those two points, technology optimist and just superstars. That's interesting.
turns.zh: 我敢打赌，技术乐观主义者和超级巨星这两类人群之间肯定有很大的重叠。这挺有意思的。

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: Yeah, there definitely is. That's actually really good. I hadn't thought about that. You're right. I think there's definitely that overlap, because folks who are in that mode, they really get around more together. I'm also an angel investor and an investor in a bunch of companies. Lenny, you and I have invested in a bunch of companies together as well. And it's like that. It's really about people who have the same kind of frequency in terms of thinking about the world outlook and they want to go on to do interesting things. I think that's really what drives the narrative forward.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实存在重叠。说得真在理。我之前都没想到这一点。你说得对。我觉得这种重叠确实存在，因为处于这种状态的人，他们确实更容易相互结交。我自己也是天使投资人，投资了不少公司。伦尼，你和我也一起投资了不少公司。就是这样。关键在于那些对世界观有着相似认知频率、渴望开创有趣事业的人。我觉得这才是推动行业发展的不竭动力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of technology optimism and technology in general, of the things that you've worked on, what would you say you're most proud of project wise, product wise, feature wise?
turns.zh: 说到技术乐观主义和科技领域，你参与过的项目中，从项目、产品或功能层面来看，你最引以为傲的是哪一个？

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: Yeah. Again, I've had just the incredible opportunity to be part of phenomenal companies that have created world changing products. I had a small, small, small part to play in that. I always emphasize that. It's not me, it was a team. And I really mean it. I'm not just saying it because I'm on your podcast, but it truly is. I'm particularly proud of the work that I did both at Google and at Uber. I'll give you a couple of examples to illustrate that point. (00:09:47): When I joined Google in India in 2008, I started off working on Google Maps and I remember how counterintuitive it was for anybody; my friends and family, a bunch of other folks whom I talked to. Counterintuitive in terms of why would anybody ever use maps on their mobile phone in India? The reason was because the norm was that, firstly, the country's unmappable because there's no good addressing system. So how do you even look at places? Then the second one was there were always people around that you can just roll down your car window and just ask people, "Hey, I'm going here and can you just give me guidance or directions?" That was the norm. That's how people navigated for a really long time. (00:10:32): When I started working on it, I think for me, my belief was, again going back to the tech optimism aspect, is why can't we in India have the same quality maps like we have in the United States? Why not? Why shouldn't we do it? Why are users here not getting the same benefit and same productivity gain, if you will, and less stress in their daily commute and things like that? (00:10:55): So we started building it. We started building the data. We went ahead and really mapped the country as much as we could. Both ourselves and through a lot of amazing work from our users who co-mapped the world with us. Over time, India became, I think, the second largest country for Google Maps in the world in terms of users. Of course, a lot of that happened because of Android. Android took off and Android had Google Maps on it. But it's just incredible to see how, in a short span of a few years, it just went up to becoming so useful. It's not that we were just distributing Google Maps on Android, people were using it. People were actually using it to go from point A to point B. (00:11:35): I feel really proud about that. I think the team did an incredible effort. It wasn't even a big team. It was a relatively small team, very passionate about going and doing this, and we made that happen. (00:11:43): Then at Uber, initially, before I took on the CPO role, I was leading maps and marketplace. When I was doing maps and marketplace, again, how do you get the ETA that you see on Uber when you open the Uber app and you request a car... The average ETA's went down to less than five minutes globally. Just think about that for a minute. In fact, it was 75 countries, more than 300 cities, if I remember correctly, where you could just open the Uber app and get an Uber in, average, less than five minutes. A lot of operational work need to happen for sure, but the technology, the marketplace technology especially to be able to connect the right rider to the right driver, have the mapping infrastructure underneath it to ensure that the car actually reaches you in that amount of time; I just feel very proud of all the work that happened during that time to make Uber really successful in terms of providing that kind of a service. (00:12:37): One fun anecdote I'll give you where my world came together and it just blows my mind even today, I remember I joined Uber in late 2015 and I made a trip to India to see my parents in sometime around 2016, 2017. I forget. It was around that time. And I was at home in Bangalore and I ordered an Uber. And the guy shows up, the driver comes in, and I sit in the back of the car. He starts the trip using the Uber app, and then he clicks Navigate and he goes to Google Maps. And I was sitting there. I was like, "Man, I built these two to a certain extent." It was just crazy to think about how two of my worlds came together at that point. I still vividly remember that moment where I felt really proud that I had a little bit of a part to play in both those products.
turns.zh:
是的。再说一次，我有幸能参与打造改变世界的产品的非凡公司。我在其中发挥的作用微乎其微，我总是强调这一点。这不是我个人的功劳，而是团队的成果。我说这话绝非客套，因为这确实如此。我尤其为自己在谷歌和优步的贡献感到自豪。我举几个例子来说明这一点。

（00:09:47）：2008年我加入印度谷歌团队时，最初负责谷歌地图项目。我记得当时大家的反应多么不可思议——无论是家人、朋友，还是其他与我交谈过的人，都觉得在印度用手机导航地图简直难以置信。原因在于印度缺乏完善的地址系统，导致人们无法准确定位地点。此外，人们习惯于摇下车窗，向路人询问路线，这也是他们长期以来的导航方式。

（00:10:32）：开始研发项目时，我秉持的信念——借用科技乐观主义的理念——是为什么印度不能拥有和美国一样高质量的地图？为什么不行？为什么不应该做？为什么这里的用户无法获得同样的益处和生产力提升，减少日常通勤压力？

（00:10:55）：于是我们着手构建数据。我们尽可能详尽地绘制印度地图，既靠团队努力，也得益于用户与我们共同完成的数据贡献。最终，印度成为全球第二大谷歌地图用户国。当然，这离不开安卓系统的推动——安卓搭载了谷歌地图。但令人惊叹的是，在短短几年间，地图服务就变得如此实用。我们并非简单地在安卓上分发谷歌地图，而是用户真正在用它导航出行。

（00:11:35）：这让我深感自豪。我认为团队付出了非凡努力。团队规模并不大，但成员充满激情，我们成功达成了目标。

（00:11:43）：在优步，担任首席产品官之前，我负责地图和市场业务。在优化地图和市场服务时，我们如何实现优步应用中显示的预计到达时间（ETA）？全球范围内，平均ETA时间缩短至不足五分钟。想想看，当时覆盖75个国家、300多个城市，只要打开优步应用，平均五分钟内就能叫到车。这背后需要大量运营支持，但技术层面——尤其是平台匹配乘客与司机的能力，以及地图基础设施保障车辆准时到达——更令人钦佩。能参与优步在服务方面的成功，我倍感荣幸。

（00:12:37）：还有个趣事至今令我震惊。2015年底加入优步后，我曾有次出行，
2016年或2017年左右，我回印度探望父母。具体时间我记不太清了，反正是在那段时间。我当时在班加罗尔的家里，叫了一辆优步。司机来后，我们坐进车里。他用优步App启动行程后，点击了导航功能，然后切换到了谷歌地图。我坐在后排，心里想：“天啊，我参与开发了这两款产品。”回想起那一刻，两个我深有感情的项目在那一刻交汇，我为自己能为这两款产品贡献一份力量而深感自豪，至今仍记忆犹新。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is some unbelievable impact. It boggles my mind how many people have been impacted by the work that you've done on the teams that you've been on. Like a billion people in India and everyone in the world using Uber. It's unreal. I would feel very proud myself, watching that experience. (00:13:41): Something people may feel when they see a career like yours, they're like, "Man, Manik's just killing it. He's done everything. Everything just is clicking, always winning." I imagine there's been a few times when you've made mistakes or things have been really challenging. What would you say has been one of the more challenging projects or points in your career?
turns.zh: 这种影响真是令人难以置信。光是想想有多少人受益于你在所属团队的工作成果，就令人惊叹不已——比如印度十亿用户，以及全球所有使用优步的人。这简直不可思议。若我亲眼见证这般成就，定会倍感自豪。（00:13:41）：当人们看到你这般辉煌的职业生涯时，或许会感叹：“天哪，马尼克简直太厉害了。他无所不能。一切都顺风顺水，总能笑到最后。” 我想你肯定也经历过犯错或面临巨大挑战的时刻。在你的职业生涯中，哪一个项目或关键时刻最具挑战性？

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: Yeah. No, absolutely. This is really important to talk about as well, because we glamorize successes and we don't talk enough about challenges. I'm really happy that you're asking this. I would give you two times which... I had a lot of learning from both of them, but they were pretty tough times for me. The first time was, I had started my own company at the height of the dotcom boom. We incorporated our company in June '99, and then in March of 2000 we sold our company to another company from Norway. That was the peak of the dotcom boom. Then within a few months right after that, we had the dotcom bust and it was terrible. Terrible. I know we have a pretty bad economy right now. There's a lot of stuff going on. It was really bad, because people around me, my friends, were losing their jobs. (00:14:52): Luckily we had some funding. We had secured some of our funding and we had had an acquisition. The parent company was pretty strong in terms of their balance sheet, so we could continue to do it. But things didn't get better, Lenny. 2000 went by, 2001 came in. We kept waiting for things to improve, but they never improved. So we had to pivot. We had to pivot as a company. My co-founders actually left the company at that point. I still wanted to be there, because I really believed that I can keep moving this company forward. Then I was working with the founders of the parent company. We pivoted multiple times, we tried a few things. I even relocated back from Singapore back to India to set up an engineering office so that we can get into a SaaS kind of a model versus an eCommerce company that we were. (00:15:35): I tried many things over those two or three years. And remember, this was my first, quote unquote, "job" out of college. I was doing a lot of that and it was a very tough time. But at the same time I learned a lot. I learned a lot about myself, I learned a lot about managing ambiguity and just keeping people motivated through a tough time. A lot of that also has to come from keeping yourself motivated, because people can smell fear and pessimism from far. Just like optimism is infectious, so is pessimism. If you're not feeling great as a leader, people will see it. Absolutely. People are not stupid. You have to not fake it. You have to really be motivated to stick it out, and that's what I tried to do at least, and I learned a lot in that. That was one really challenging time for me. (00:16:21): Then the second one was, man, during Uber. 2017, 2018 was crazy at Uber. Oh my God. There were just so much going on with leadership changes, with the brand issues we were getting. For me, there were times when I would commute up from my house to the office, and while I'm in the car I will be listening to some news or whatever and I'll hear about things that happened at Uber that day from the news before I got to hear it from within the company. It was that crazy during that time. So again, a lot of chaos, a lot of churn at the company as well. It was something where you just had to keep your head down and just keep staying focused on what the core is. (00:17:03): I think that is where, Lenny, the optimism in me in terms of, what am I really doing? Is this a service that really benefits millions of people around the world? Are we creating true change? Those are things that I just have to dig deep into to make sure that I stay grounded on why am I here and why I remain to be here and then at the same time motivate my team. But yeah, those were the two really challenging times that I have encountered, at least in my career.
turns.zh: 是的。没错，绝对重要。谈论这些问题也很有必要，因为我们总是美化成功，却很少提及挑战。我很高兴你能提出这个问题。我会分享两个经历……从这两段经历中，我都收获良多，但它们对我来说都是非常艰难的时期。第一次是在互联网泡沫高峰期，我创办了自己的公司。1999 年 6 月注册公司，2000 年 3 月就把公司卖给了挪威的一家公司。当时正值互联网泡沫顶峰。然而几个月后，泡沫破裂，情况急转直下。（00:14:52）当时身边的朋友都失业了，经济环境也很糟糕。第二次是在 Uber 时期。2017 年和 2018 年简直疯狂，领导层变动、品牌危机层出不穷。有时我开车从家到公司，新闻里播报的 Uber 最新动态比公司内部得知的还要早。整个时期乱成一团，但我始终专注核心业务。（00:17:03）这两次经历让我深刻认识到，必须坚定信念：我要为数百万用户创造真正的价值，推动真正的变革。这些时刻考验着我的定力，同时也激励着团队。这些挑战让我明白，保持乐观、正直和专注是领导者的必备品质。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Those are awesome examples. I imagine a lot of founders are going through a lot of challenging times right now with the market, and imagine these experiences for you were really important and impacted your ability to take on bigger roles and bigger challenges in the future. Is that how you see it? These are important experiences to have over time as a product leader and just leader in general?
turns.zh: 这些都是很棒的例子。我想很多创业者目前正面临着市场挑战，而这些经历对你们来说非常重要，也影响了你们未来承担更大角色、迎接更大挑战的能力。你是这么看的吗？作为产品负责人，乃至整个领导团队，随着时间推移积累这些经验非常重要。

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: Oh, absolutely. Because like I said, you learn a lot about yourself when you go through a situation like this. You learn both things that bother you or bring you down, and things that give you energy. It's sometimes counterintuitive to think about this. When you're going through a bad time, often then people will say, "Well, during a bad time I only learned things which are bad." But you also learn things that are good. Which is, maybe during a bad time you did something and you suddenly felt relieved or energized, and then you look at that and say, "Wait, I should do more of that even during a good time, because can you imagine the compounding power that I would get? Because stuff is good and I'm doing this and I'll feel even better." (00:18:26): I learned a lot in terms of my own personal energy, things that get me going, things that really stop me in my tracks. And at the same time, how do you work with a team? How do you motivate them? How do you keep your head down and focus, versus getting distracted? What are some of the decisions you make around your product roadmap? (00:18:47): I'll give you an example. During my startup, when we were going through that, in order to motivate the team, one of the best tricks that I came up with, and I learned this from a bunch of other people also, is you just give a team a win. Winning really, really drives a lot of energy. We had a choice to make between launching something which will take six months, versus launching something that we can launch in a very small-ish kind of way, but launch it in a month. And we chose the latter, because when we did that, I remember people were giving high five to each other, people were saying, "Hey, you know what? This is great. We put something in front of customers." We had, I think, 10 customers who used it or something, because we were so soft-scaling that feature. But that didn't really matter. The point was that you get confidence from getting things out, putting it out there, and you feel good about being a builder and being someone who is actually creating a difference. That really grounds the team and focuses the team that there is some real value here. (00:19:45): Some of those things I picked up. Both going through that turbulent time, I picked up. And I have used that even in good times to make sure that we keep building good products.
turns.zh: 哦，绝对没错。正如我所说，当你经历这样的情况时，你会对自己有更深刻的认识。你会发现哪些事情让你感到困扰或情绪低落，哪些事情能给你带来能量。有时候这看似违背直觉。当你处于低谷时，人们常说：“嗯，糟糕的时候我只学到了坏东西。” 但你也能学到好的东西。比如在低谷时期，你做某件事后突然感到释然或充满活力，然后你会意识到：“等等，我甚至在顺境时也应该多做这样的事，因为你能想象这会带来多大的复利效应吗？因为这些好习惯能让我感觉更好。”（00:18:26）：我从个人能量层面学到了很多，哪些事情能让我充满动力，哪些事情会让我停滞不前。同时，你如何与团队合作？如何激励他们？如何保持专注而非分心？在产品路线图方面又做了哪些决策？（00:18:47）：我举个例子。在我的创业公司经历低谷时，为了激励团队，我想到了一个很棒的策略，也是从其他人那里学到的，那就是给团队一个胜利时刻。胜利感真的能极大激发能量。我们面临一个选择：是花六个月时间推出某个产品，还是以较小规模、一个月内就能上线的产品先试水。最终我们选择了后者，因为当我们这么做时，记得大家互相击掌庆祝，说：“嘿，你知道吗？太棒了。我们让产品接触到了用户。” 虽然只有大概10个用户在用，但这真的不重要。关键是把产品推向市场能给你带来信心，让你感受到作为建设者、创造价值者的满足感。这能让团队扎根，专注于创造真正的价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a good tactical tip. Find a win. Keep people motivated. Speaking of wins, coming back to Google Maps and Uber, they're probably two of the most widely used, successful consumer products in the world. I don't know if I can think of other products that are used by more people for this long. Then now at Microsoft you're helping Microsoft get more into consumer on the communications side. I imagine you know a thing or two about building successful consumer apps, and so I want to ask a couple questions along those lines. What are two or three surprising or counterintuitive things that you've learned about building consumer products?
turns.zh: 这真是个很棒的策略技巧。找到胜利时刻，保持团队动力。说到胜利时刻，再回到谷歌地图和优步，它们可能是全球使用最广泛、最成功的消费级产品。我想不出还有其他产品能被更多人长期使用这么久。现在在微软，你正帮助微软在通信领域深耕消费市场。我想你对打造成功的消费级应用颇有心得，所以我想围绕这个话题问几个问题。打造消费级产品时，你学到的哪些令人惊讶或违背直觉的经验？

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: The good news is that there's just... Because of Twitter and a bunch of other channels, including your newsletter by the way, I feel like people are very well informed these days. And I love that. (00:20:43): Let me digress for a second and then I'll come back to your question. One thing that I'm observing a lot, Lenny, which I feel very, very happy about, is the quality of learning and insights and frameworks and best practices is so universal at this point. It used to be that you had to be in the Valley or being part of a small group of folks who are doing things at the cutting edge to have those crazy insights about how do you find product market fit and do all that kind of stuff. Today I talk to people from all over the world for various reasons, and it's incredible how fast people pick up all these insights and frameworks and then they apply them to their local setting and so on. I find that to be one of the most wonderful things ever. (00:21:32): I think folks like you have obviously played a big part, because you have global subscribers and you share some of the best practices. But just generally, that's actually a really good thing for the world, that people have so much access to clarity of thinking. And the best people are actually putting themselves out there, which is great. (00:21:47): In terms of the counterintuitive stuff, I think two things. One is building consumer products is very hard. I think people think it's easy, because each of us is a consumer. We think of ourselves as a good user, we think of our friends as users, we think of our family as users. And we say, "Well, if we just build it for ourselves and for our family and friends..." By the way, a lot of great consumer products started that way, so I'm not saying don't do that. But man, it's hard. It takes a long time to get things right. Because you're essentially trying to get so many things right when you're building a successful consumer product. You have to be able to reach out to a vast, heterogeneous set of users who have different needs, who have different perspectives. The go to market is always very interesting, because you can't force people to use your product. People have to choose you, you don't choose them. That's the part where... How do you drive virality? How do you drive that real love for a consumer product? And it has to create real value. (00:22:52): The other thing about time is that, in order for you to find product market fit and then scale from there, you just have to try a lot of different things. There are theoretical playbooks around it, but you got to just get into it. Going back to the point I was making earlier about wins, get some wins and see the results and then iterate from there. I think it's just hard and it takes a lot longer than what people imagine consumer products do. Versus, let's say, enterprise products or products of other nature. That's one counterintuitive thing that at least I've learned. (00:23:21): The second one is the global patterns that you see in consumer products in terms of the user interface; the core things that people do or expect. At this point along of that is pretty universal. There's always this debate where people would say, "Well, need to have one product for the U.S., another different type of product for Asia, another different type of product for Africa. I think we are past that point. That's again another counterintuitive thing, where people spend a little too much... I've seen this in many companies. People spend too much time debating that, "Oh, the users in market X are different." Well yes, they're different, but they use the product the same way. (00:24:02): That's the part which I think... And I'm not making an argument against localization. Of course you need localization around language, pricing. There are some legal requirements, all of that stuff. Obviously you have to do that, otherwise you don't even have a right to exist in that market. But by and large the patterns are very similar. You look at global products, even like Facebook or Google Search or Maps or Twitter or TikTok and so on, all of them have a similar pattern or similar app for the entire world, and they keep on innovating or localizing at the edges. (00:24:33): That's the other counterintuitive thing that people should know about consumer products. Build for the world from day one. Understand that there are going to be some nuances that you'll have to solve as you drive adoption in certain markets, but don't over index on building market specific solutions, because consumers have moved on from that kind of a model. Those are the two, in terms of product building, counterintuitive trends at least I have picked up over the years.
turns.zh:
好消息是，情况确实如此……得益于推特等诸多平台，包括你的新闻通讯，我觉得如今人们获取信息的渠道比以往任何时候都多。我对此深感欣慰。（00:20:43）：容我稍作偏题，再回归你的问题。莱尼，我注意到一个非常积极的现象——学习资源、洞察见解、框架方法和最佳实践如今已变得如此普及。这在过去是不可想象的——你必须身处硅谷，或是加入一小群处于行业前沿的从业者，才有机会接触到那些关于如何找到产品市场契合点等前沿洞见。如今，我因各种原因与世界各地的人交流，他们能如此迅速地掌握这些见解并将其应用于本地环境，这实在令人惊叹。我认为这是当今世界最美好的现象之一。

（00:21:32）：我觉得像你这样的人显然发挥了重要作用，因为你拥有全球订阅用户，并分享最佳实践。但从更宏观的角度来看，这对全世界来说都是极好的事情——人们能如此轻松获取清晰的思维框架。最优秀的人才正积极分享他们的智慧，这实在难能可贵。

（00:21:47）：至于那些反直觉的挑战，我想主要有两点：一是打造消费级产品极其困难。人们往往认为这很简单，因为我们都是消费者。我们自视为优秀用户，把朋友和家人也视为用户，并心想：“只要为自己、家人和朋友打造产品……”诚然，许多伟大的消费级产品正是如此起步的，我并非反对这种做法。但这实在不易。想要把产品做好，需要耗费大量时间。因为要打造成功的消费级产品，必须同时兼顾多个方面：覆盖广泛而多元的用户群体，他们有着不同的需求和视角。市场推广环节也极具挑战性——你无法强制用户使用产品，用户必须主动选择你，而非你去选择用户。这正是如何激发病毒式传播、如何让用户真正爱上产品所在的关键。产品还必须创造真正的价值。

（00:22:52）：关于时间维度，要找到产品市场契合点并实现规模化扩张，关键在于不断尝试。理论上有相关指南，但实践中必须亲身投入。回归我之前提到的成功秘诀——先取得一些成果，观察效果，再据此迭代。我认为这条路比人们想象的要艰难得多，比打造企业级产品或其他类型的产品耗时得多。这至少是我学到的反直觉之处。

（00:23:21）：第二个反直觉观点是，消费级产品在用户界面和核心功能方面的全球模式趋于一致。目前仍有争论声称：“美国市场需要一款产品，亚洲市场需要另一款，非洲市场又需要另一款。” 我认为这种时代已然落伍。这再次印证了反直觉的观点——人们往往在无谓地纠结于“某个市场用户不同”之类的问题。
是的，它们确实有所不同，但用户使用产品的方式却如出一辙。（00:24:02）：这正是我所认为的……我并非反对本地化。当然，在语言、定价等方面，进行本地化是必要的。还有一些法律要求之类的，这些都是必须要做的，否则你根本没有在该市场立足的资格。但总体而言，产品模式是高度相似的。看看全球性的产品，比如Facebook、谷歌搜索、地图、推特、抖音等，它们在全球范围内都采用了相似的模式或应用程序，并且在边缘领域持续创新或进行本地化。（00:24:33）：这是关于消费品领域另一个违背直觉的现象。产品从一开始就应该面向全球市场开发。要明白，在某些市场推广产品时，确实会遇到一些需要解决的细微问题，但不要过度依赖开发针对特定市场的解决方案，因为消费者已经不再青睐这种模式。至少从我多年积累的经验来看，以上两点是产品开发领域中最值得注意的反直觉趋势。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Unit. What did Gusto, Uber, Shopify, and AngelList all have in common? They've all decided to build banking into their product. According to AngelList head of product, banking makes every single feature more interesting. With it our platform functions as financial mission control for our customers.
