turns.zh: 本期节目由Unit赞助。Gusto、Uber、Shopify和AngelList这四家公司有什么共同点？它们都决定将银行服务功能融入自身产品。AngelList产品负责人表示，银行服务能让每一项功能更具吸引力。有了银行服务，我们的平台就能成为客户的财务指挥中心；若没有银行服务，我们不过是堆积如山的软件工具中的一员。将银行服务嵌入产品不仅能提升差异化竞争力，还能助力客户获取、留存并实现变现。Unit是银行即服务领域的市场领导者，整合多家银行合作伙伴与开发者友好型API，让各类规模的企业都能在数周内上线账户、卡片、支付和借贷功能。AngelList、IB、Invoice2Go和Roofstock等头部品牌都信赖Unit的技术。若想了解Unit如何助力像您这样的公司构建银行服务体系，请访问unit.co/lenny申请演示或体验免费沙盒环境。网址是unit.co/lenny。（00:26:04）：在本次对话之前，我们探讨了大公司产品适配的理念，即如何在大公司内部开发新产品。您能否进一步阐述这一思路？

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. I've been noodling a lot on this, especially since I took on my role at Microsoft as well. And prior to that, even at Google, this was always an interesting discussion. Let's say you are building a new product or leading a new project, if you will, at a larger company. In fact, this also applies to medium-sized companies. I wouldn't say for startups, but medium-sized companies. Usually the narrative in the room when you're discussing this with your team and with your leadership team would be, "Okay, we got to go find product market fit." Absolutely. Yeah. We have to do a bunch of stuff, as we just talked about. Consumer products take time. All of that stuff. (00:26:57): But I think there's a question before that question, which is how do you find company product fit? What I define as company product fit. Which is a company essentially is a portfolio of products, and every large company, medium-sized company also has a portfolio. They'll have 10, 20, in some cases hundreds of products in the portfolio. Every company has unique strengths and weaknesses. This is pretty tried, but it's obvious. And I would encourage a lot of folks, when they start embarking on this journey where they're trying to really build out products and so on, is to ask that question. How does that product, assuming it's successful... If it is not successful, it doesn't matter anyway. But assuming it's successful, does it actually serve the right place in a company's product portfolio? Or not? And if it doesn't, don't do it. Why waste time? (00:27:57): Oftentimes companies will be like, "I want to do this because some other company is doing it." That is not a good reason. You should only invest in products, or projects for that matter, because you can play to your strengths and you can create some unique consumer, customer value. And by the way, you can do it better than anybody else out there. That's what I mean by company product fit. Take that first step and understand does this even resonate and is it part of the portfolio? Does it make sense? (00:28:26): Because if you can answer that question with enough conviction, then your road to the next step on finding product market fit becomes much easier, because you don't have distractions then. Everybody gets it. Everybody gets this is a strategic effort. You have the right sponsorship at the right levels in the company, and you're executing towards it and you're finding it out. Let's say things don't go well. That's okay. People will step in to help. A lot of that will happen, because people innately get it. That this is the right product to go after from a company product fit perspective. That's something that I've been thinking a lot about and also executing as we move forward.
turns.zh: 是的，绝对正确。我对此思考了很多，尤其是在我加入微软之后。甚至在此之前，在谷歌工作时，这也是一个备受讨论的话题。假设你在一家大公司（实际上这也适用于中型公司）开发新产品或领导新项目。通常，当你与团队和领导层讨论这个问题时，会议上的主流观点会是：“好吧，我们得去寻找产品与市场的契合点。”没错，我们需要做很多工作，正如我们刚刚讨论的那样。消费级产品需要时间。所有这些步骤……（00:26:57）但我认为，在这个问题之前还有一个更深层的疑问——如何找到公司产品与市场的契合点？我所定义的公司产品契合点，本质上是公司作为一个产品组合的集合。每家大公司、中型公司都有这样的产品组合。它们的产品组合中可能包含10个、20个，甚至数百个产品。每家公司都有独特的优势和劣势。这听起来老生常谈，但确实是常识。我想鼓励许多刚开始踏上产品开发之路的人，多问问自己这个问题：假设这个产品成功了……即使不成功也无妨，但假设它成功了，它在公司的产品组合中是否占据了合适的位置？如果没有，那就别做了。何必浪费时间呢？（00:27:57）很多公司会说：“因为其他公司在做，所以我们也要做。” 这不是一个好的理由。你只应该投资于那些能发挥自身优势、能为消费者创造独特价值的产品或项目。顺便说一句，你应该比市场上任何人都做得更好。这就是我所说的公司产品契合点。迈出第一步，了解这个产品是否能引起共鸣，是否属于产品组合？是否合理？（00:28:26）因为如果你能以足够坚定的信念回答这个问题，那么你找到产品市场契合点的下一步之路就会容易得多，因为你不会再被干扰。每个人都能理解这是一项战略性努力。在公司内部，你得到了合适层级的支持，大家都朝着这个目标努力并不断验证。即使事情进展不顺利，也没关系。人们会介入帮忙的。因为人们天生就能理解，从公司产品契合的角度来看，这是值得追逐的正确产品。这是我一直在思考并在未来不断践行的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of that gone wrong that you can share? Whether it's a company you've worked at or a company you've seen do it badly.
turns.zh: 你能否分享一个失败的案例？无论是自己工作过的公司，还是你见过的做得不好的公司。

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: I'll have to think through specific examples, but companies do this all the time, where they do these line extensions. Where they'll say, "Well, we have a lot of traction in a particular segment. Why don't we just go to an adjacent segment? If we just add two more features, suddenly this will be appealing to an adjacent segment." A classic example would be you're doing something for, I don't know, small and medium businesses and you say, "Well, now I just have to add two more features and now I'm going to go up market and I'll get to compete in the enterprise." Or it could be the other way around too, where you have something in the enterprise business and you want to suddenly go down market to SMB. (00:29:44): In my view, it's hard. Because again, the capabilities that you need, the thinking that you need, is something you have to really be clear about. This is not to say that it will not fit in the company's portfolio. It's just that when you're making a choice like that, make sure you set it up well to succeed. That's the other part of the equation as well.
turns.zh:
我得仔细想想具体例子，但企业经常会这样做——推出产品线延伸产品。他们会说：“嗯，我们在某个细分市场已经取得了不错的发展，为什么不拓展到相邻的细分市场呢？只要再增加两个功能，产品就能吸引到相邻的目标客户群体了。” 一个典型的例子是，你原本专注于中小型企业市场，后来你会说：“现在只要再增加两个功能，我就能向上拓展至企业级市场，与大企业竞争了。” 反之亦然，比如你原本专注于企业级市场，现在却想下探至中小型企业市场。  

（00:29:44）在我看来，这很难。因为你需要具备的能力、需要运用的思维方式，都必须清晰明确。这并不是说这种策略不适合公司的业务组合，只是当你做出这样的决策时，必须确保策略设计得当、成功的可能性最大。这也是成功的关键因素之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of setting it up to succeed, you also have this idea of a consumer stack concept that I think you've been talking about at Microsoft. Can you talk about what that's all about?
turns.zh: 说到策略设计，您还提到了消费者堆栈（consumer stack）的概念，我记得您在微软曾谈到过这个概念。能否请您解释一下这个概念的核心含义？

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: Yeah, sure. One of the things that I'm doing at Microsoft right now is, while I'm working on a lot of the consumer communication products, the other thing that I'm really helping the company think about is how do we get more at scale consumer products built at Microsoft. Part of this is just distilling some of the learnings that I've had over the years. I think there are like five things that I would talk about, which I call the consumer stack, which is essentially a set of capabilities that companies need to have a good chance of success at building a consumer product. Remember, nobody can give a playbook to build a successful consumer product. That does not exist. Because as we were discussing earlier, it's so fickle and so many things have to go right for you to build a successful consumer product. But at least you have a set of capabilities, so you set yourself up the best. (00:31:01): The first one I would say is around design-led thinking to delight users. Going back to your days at Airbnb, Lenny, I'm sure this is something that resonates with you. Design for consumer products is such a critical part of how you build the right pull from consumers these days. Poorly designed products have no chance at this point. Your craftsmanship and the design capabilities have to be A plus. And if you don't have that, then you should really invest in that. This is not just about having the best designers. Of course you should. It's just the thinking. It's a attention to detail. It's the attention to how things are pixel to pixel, moving from one screen to another screen and so on. You really have to sweat it out and really be clear in terms of how it's adding value to a consumer. That is, I think, a core capability in these days to build a consumer product. That's number one. (00:31:54): Number two is strong focus and prioritization. You can apply strong focus and prioritization to anything in life, but I think it's even more important for consumer products. Because oftentimes people, when they think about solving a problem, they think about coming up with 20 features at the same time, and it's not needed. You don't need 20 features to solve a problem. You just need one or two features which work really well. This whole concept of critical user journeys. How do you make sure that, if you're solving problem X, any feature that you build in the product... Firstly your product should have very few features in the beginning. But even if it has those features, it should be well designed and it should have the focus and prioritization so that you're only getting things for the critical journey so that the user can use it and not get confused. That's the second one. (00:32:38): Most PMs totally understand that. That's their job description, to focus and prioritize. But I feel like a lot of times the PMs do get very confused and distracted, because the number of ideas that people have is so large that they want to just throw everything into the product, and that doesn't work. You have to keep a very high bar for focus and prioritization. That's capability number two. (00:33:00): Number three is having the right metrics and instrumentation. This talks to the data aspect of the culture, which is, if you don't have the metric with regards to what you're optimizing for at the initial state of the product, middle state of the product, late stage of the product, you're just not going to choose the right things. How will you measure success? How will you convince yourself, your team, and broader stakeholders that this is actually working or not working? Having the right metrics is important, but it's incredible how many times people have the metrics but they don't instrument them. They'll have all these debates, because the product is not instrumented properly. And everybody will talk about the same metric, but they'll have different nuances in terms of, "Oh, what does it really mean? What is a daily active user? Okay, daily means... Okay, I understand it's on a daily basis. What is active?" And there'll be debates about what is active. Pick a definition, instrument it, codify it. No confusion. That's number three. (00:33:59): Number four is more on the engineering side, which is how do you get to a very high ship velocity, and the ability to experiment and learn fast. At a broader level, especially during the initial phases, if you're not learning, you are really not doing anything well. You've got to be learning. You've got to be learning good things, bad things, doesn't matter. You've got to be learning. Having the experimentation velocity, having a building culture where engineers are able to check in code, see the results, and then quickly come into another release and stuff like that, I think that's really important for a consumer product. (00:34:29): Finally, underpinning all of this is just having strong talent. Assess your talent; your product talent, your design talent, your data talent, your engineering talent, your marketing talent, all these functions. You just have to have a talented pool of people who like to build stuff, and they're the people who understand and have the empathy for consumers. (00:34:50): To me, I think these five capabilities... And as a leader, or product leader, or an engineering leader, or anyone who's basically responsible for running products in small company, big company, medium-sized company, it doesn't matter; if you're in the consumer space, my thinking here is that if you look at these five categories and five capabilities, you should really have a report card and say, "Okay. How do I rate these?" If I were to look at my own team, what do I think about design thinking? What do I think about strong focus and prioritization? Are we doing an A job? Are we doing a B job? Are doing a C job or D job? I would argue that if you get to an A job over time, because not everybody will be at A on day one, but if you get that over time, I think you will start seeing results which are very meaningful. That's how I've been thinking about the consumer stack.
turns.zh:
是的，当然可以。我目前在微软的工作重点之一，是在致力于多个面向消费者的通讯产品之余，协助公司思考如何在微软内部打造更多大规模的消费级产品。这其中部分工作就是总结我多年来积累的经验。我认为有五个关键点值得探讨，我称之为"消费者产品堆栈"——这是一套帮助企业提升成功几率的核心能力组合。请记住，没有任何现成的成功秘籍。正如我们之前讨论的，打造成功的消费级产品本质上是件易变的事，需要诸多因素完美契合。但至少你得具备这些核心能力，这样才能为成功奠定最佳基础。

（00:31:01）：第一个要点是以设计为核心的用户体验创新。伦尼，你在Airbnb的经历肯定对此深有体会。如今，设计已成为打造消费级产品的核心竞争力。设计不佳的产品根本没有胜算。精湛的工艺和设计能力必须达到A+级水准。如果你缺乏这些能力，就应该加以投资。这不仅仅是拥有顶尖设计师那么简单——关键在于设计思维、对细节的执着，以及对产品界面连贯性的把控。必须精心打磨每个像素，确保用户价值清晰传递。这才是当今打造消费级产品的核心能力。

（00:31:54）：第二点是高度聚焦与优先级管理。这种能力适用于生活中的方方面面，但在消费级产品中尤为重要。许多人试图同时开发20项功能，却发现这根本行不通。解决问题只需一两项核心功能即可。关键在于聚焦核心用户路径，确保产品中的每项功能都紧扣核心路径，让用户无需困惑即可完成任务。这是第二个核心要素。

（00:32:38）：大多数产品经理都深知聚焦与优先级管理是职责所在，但现实中他们常因创意过剩而迷失方向。必须设定高标准的聚焦与优先级管理标准。这是第二项核心能力。

（00:33:00）：第三点是构建有效的数据监测体系。数据驱动的文化至关重要。如果产品初期、中期、末期都缺乏优化指标，决策就难免偏差。如何衡量成功？如何说服团队和利益相关者产品是否有效？
拥有正确的指标固然重要，但令人惊讶的是，许多人明明有指标却不进行数据采集。他们会就产品问题展开激烈讨论，原因往往在于产品未能正确设置数据采集机制。大家对同一个指标争论不休，却对其含义存在诸多歧义——比如“每日活跃用户”到底意味着什么？每日意味着什么？好吧，我理解是按日统计，但活跃的定义又是什么？围绕活跃用户定义的争论层出不穷。选定一个定义，进行数据采集并形成规范，这样才能避免混淆。这就是第三条经验。  
（00:33:59）第四条经验更多聚焦于工程层面，即如何实现极高的产品发布速度，以及快速实验与学习的能力。更宏观层面而言，尤其是在初期阶段，如果不持续学习，那就根本无法做好产品。必须不断学习——无论是好的经验还是失败教训。拥有实验迭代的速度、构建让工程师能快速提交代码、查看结果并迅速进入下一个发布周期的文化，我认为这对消费级产品至关重要。  
（00:34:29）最后，支撑这一切的核心是拥有优秀的人才。评估你的产品人才、设计人才、数据人才、工程人才、市场营销人才等各个职能部门。你必须拥有一支热爱产品开发、理解并共情用户需求的卓越团队。  
（00:34:50）对我而言，这五项核心能力……作为产品负责人、工程负责人，或任何负责消费级产品的小、中、大型公司的管理者——无论规模大小——如果你审视这五大类别与五项核心能力，就应该制定一份评估表格并自问：“我在这方面表现如何？”以我自己的团队为例，我如何看待设计思维？如何看待高度专注和优先级管理？我们是A级表现吗？B级？C级还是D级？我相信只要能逐步达到A级水准（毕竟并非所有人都能一开始就达标），最终就能收获显著成效。这就是我对消费级产品全栈的理解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I was going to ask how you operationalize this. It sounds like it's going to turn into Manik's consumer stack scorecard, and bigger companies can leverage this at their own company and show their manager, "Hey, we're moving really slowly. Maybe this is an area we should focus before we bet big on consumer."
turns.zh: 太棒了。我本来想问你是怎么把这套方法落地的。听起来这会变成马尼克（Manik）的消费者堆栈评分卡，而大公司可以借鉴这一框架，向自己的经理展示：“嘿，我们进展太慢了。或许我们应该先专注于这块领域，再考虑大规模投入消费者业务。”

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: Yeah. I'm trying to operationalize this myself right now in my current job, and I have used some version of this. I mean, this is not something I just came up with. It's something that has been in my mind for a while. I've used it in some shape or form. But during my break, especially before I joined Microsoft, I think this came together for me as something a little bit more tangible that I can use. Then I started applying it, so I think it's been pretty interesting to see.
turns.zh: 是啊。我现在的工作中也在尝试把这套方法落地，我之前也用过类似的版本。说实话，这不是我突发奇想出来的东西，而是我思考已久的概念。之前也用过类似的框架，但在休假期间，尤其是在加入微软之前，这套框架在我脑海中逐渐成形，变得更加具体可行。然后我开始应用它，看到效果真是挺有意思的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I'm hoping that this proliferates through larger companies and becomes a thing that we can root back to this chat. (00:36:23): Shifting a little bit to the CPO role and the VP of product role that you've had at a few companies, in theory this is kind of an end state for a product leader. Every PM, if they stay down the PM career track, they'll become a CPO or VP of product or head of product somewhere. A couple of questions here. One is, do you have a sense of how many PMs actually stay on this track and end up in one of these roles, versus move on to some other role or place?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我希望这套方法能在大公司里广泛推广，成为我们可以追溯到这次对话的成果。（00:36:23）：接下来聊聊你曾在几家公司担任的首席产品官（CPO）和产品副总裁（VP of Product）职位。从理论上讲，这是产品领导者的终极目标。每个产品经理，如果坚持走产品经理的职业路线，最终都会成为某个公司的CPO、VP of Product或产品负责人。有几个问题想请教：你是否了解有多少产品经理最终走上这条职业道路，进入这些职位，而不是转向其他角色或领域？

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: Yeah. That's a great question. I would say that the percentage for CPO in particular, you having a C title and being a CPO, I think that percentage is still relatively small. This is just my sense. I haven't done the numbers to give you a more accurate picture here, but I think my sense is relatively smaller. Because I think a large part of it depends on how companies are organized. Companies can be organized functionally, companies can be organized through business units, and oftentimes these days it's a mix of both. If you look at any company, they'll have some C level functional executives, but underneath them they'll have GMs. The organization design is just such an evolving field always. And as they say, companies will go one... they'll swing the pendulum one way and they'll say, "Oh, over time it's not working," and then they'll swing the pendulum the other way and then they keep going back and forth. I think the percentage for CPO in particularly in my mind is probably not as big as what people think it is. Like I said, because of the way that companies are organized. (00:37:50): I think the interesting thing here is I am just seeing personally, having been a CPO myself and also talking to a lot of people in my network and just observing a bunch of different companies, I think the CPO role is evolving. Or the head of product role is also evolving. I think a lot of it is morphing more into the GM model where you're running not just product management but also perhaps PM and engineering, and design to a certain extent and data science too. You're essentially becoming the overall technical product leader at the company. (00:38:27): The reason why I feel that is happening is because it's all about accountability. It's about who has the single threaded leadership model where this person can make all the decisions when it comes to trade offs and running the roadmaps and all of that kind of stuff. It's not ideal, by the way, in all cases. Because what that means is, for somebody to be doing that, that person has to be really, really good at all those other functions too so that everyone who is in their organization respects that. Otherwise people feel like I'm the second class citizen in this model where this person doesn't know anything about, whatever; my function and so on. So it's harder, but I do feel that for optimization around decision making, around having a single threaded leadership and accountability, I feel like that's the direction where the product leadership role itself is going more and more. At least based on my experience.
turns.zh: 是的。这确实是个好问题。我想说，特别是CPO这个职位——你拥有C级头衔，同时担任CPO，我认为这个比例仍然相对较小。这只是我的感觉。我没有具体统计数据来给出更准确的数据，但我觉得我的感觉是相对较小的。因为我认为这在很大程度上取决于公司的组织架构。公司可以按职能部门组织，也可以按业务单元组织，而如今很多公司是两者的混合体。如果你观察任何一家公司，他们都会有一些C级职能高管，但在他们之下会有总经理。组织设计领域始终在不断演变。正如人们所说，公司会先朝一个方向发展，然后又反向调整，如此反复。我认为CPO这个职位在我的印象中可能并不像人们想象的那么常见。就像我说的，这取决于公司的组织方式。（00:37:50）：我觉得有趣的是，我个人观察到，既当过CPO，也和很多圈内人交流过，还观察过很多不同公司，我发现CPO这个角色正在演变。或者说产品负责人这个角色也在演变。我觉得很多职位正逐渐向总经理模式转变，你不仅要管理产品，还可能要管理项目管理、工程团队，在一定程度上还要管理设计和数据科学。基本上你要成为公司整体的技术产品负责人。（00:38:27）：我觉得这种趋势之所以出现，是因为责任归属问题。关键在于谁能拥有单线式领导模式，即在权衡取舍、制定路线图等事务上能独自做决定的人。这并不意味着在所有情况下都是理想的。因为要做到这一点，这个人必须在其他所有职能上都非常出色，这样才能让团队成员尊重他。否则人们会觉得自己在这个模式中是二等公民，觉得产品负责人对自己的职能一无所知等等。这很难做到，但我确实认为为了优化决策过程，建立单线式领导和问责机制，我觉得产品领导角色正朝着这个方向发展。这至少是基于我的经验得出的结论。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is your sense that maybe CPO might fade away as a title and GMs become the common path across companies?
turns.zh: 您是否认为CPO这个头衔可能会逐渐消失，而总经理会成为各公司的普遍职位？

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: If you were to push me on this, I would say that's probably the direction we will go. I think it's interesting to also think about CTO. If you look at the CTO roles versus SVP of engineering or a VP of engineering, I think it's an interesting debate too, what's happening with CTO roles. If a company is organized purely functionally, I think that's absolutely the right call. But as companies are changing and thinking about how they drive more accountability and more business units and so on, I just feel it probably will become more GM oriented. That does not mean that the VP product is going to go away or the VP engineering is going to go away. I think those roles will still stay. But the C-level title, reporting into the CEO but you're just running that one function; if I look at over time, maybe that role is lot less prevalent than what we have right now.
turns.zh: 如果你非要追问，我会说这很可能是我们未来的发展方向。我觉得探讨首席技术官（CTO）的角色也很有意思。对比CTO与工程副总裁（SVP）或工程副总监（VP）的职位，我认为CTO角色的演变值得深入探讨。如果一家公司纯粹按职能划分部门，我认为这是完全合理的做法。但随着企业不断变革，致力于强化业务部门的问责制等，我觉得CTO的角色可能会向首席执行官（GM）级别靠拢。这并不意味着产品副总裁或工程副总监会消失——这些职位仍将存在。但CTO这种向CEO汇报却只负责单一职能的角色，随着时间推移，或许会比现在更为罕见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you think that's partly because there's this weird overlap between CPO and CEO, and there's often tension of who's leading the product? Is that something you've seen?
turns.zh: 你认为这部分是因为首席产品官（CPO）与CEO之间存在奇怪的职能重叠，导致产品负责人角色存在权力争夺吗？你有没有遇到过这种情况？

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: Yeah. I think that's definitely an interesting one as well. I mean, if you think about it, just based on my experience, what does the CPO really do? What is their job description? I think it's useful to think through that. Generally speaking, and again, we can always talk in generalizations because that's how you should think. And every company is unique. But generally you would say the CPO is responsible for driving the product vision for the company, and that product vision cannot be divorced from the company vision. Oftentimes this is actually what also creates conflict within the leadership team, where the product vision is... people are coming up with these grandiose plans. Like, "Oh, we'll do this, we'll do that," but then it's not really grounded in the reality of where the company is. Anyways, it's around product vision and making sure it's coherent with the company vision. (00:41:09): Then the second big part of a CPO job is execution of the roadmap on the priorities. People sometimes think that, hey, I get to a C-level position. I don't have to worry about execution. Absolutely not. If you're a CPO in particular, even the CTO and the head of engineering, execution matters a lot. The operational excellence. Because things are so complex. I mean, we are in a situation where a lot of people are working remotely, there are all these different tool sets, there are all these different technologies that are coming up, you have different competitors. Execution is super important. And if people don't understand that that's a big part of their job when they get to the senior level, I think they're mistaken. The execution is another one. (00:41:50): The third is, for a CPO, especially for a tech company, because you are really driving the product roadmap, it's a very leveraged job. Meaning you have to really work with all your other peers, whether the marketing person, or the sales person, or the business unit person and so on, and just make sure that you are really even deeply connected in terms of what is really needed, so that your product roadmap is how things are going to actually come to life. It's a very cross-functional, on steroids kind of job in that sense. (00:42:19): In terms of the CEO, CPO, I think the important thing again is... And this is actually advice I've given to CEOs of some companies as well, when they first start looking for a VP of product or a CPO. This is almost like a questionnaire that I give them. The first question I ask the CEO is, what do you want to do? That's the most important question. Because a lot of times the CEO has either been the technical founder, or they have been the product founder. They can be a sales founder too. All that is fine. But what do you want to spend your time on? Because if you are going to get a CPO or a VP of product and then still want to own the product roadmap and own the execution, then don't do that. Because what is that person going to do? That's the first question that I tend to clarify between a CEO who's looking for a CPO or VP of product. (00:43:10): Then the other thing is really about, are you trying to optimize for process? Are you optimizing for strategy? Are you optimizing for team building and attraction? I think that's a really big one. Sometimes you have to get the right level of leader to attract more talent to the team. Because people say, "Oh, this person is working there. Now I want to go work in their organization." How do you think about engineering and data science and design? How do you think about GM and operations? There are a bunch of all these things in terms of the design that you need to do before you decide whether VP of product, CPO is somebody you want to get and what kind of person you want to get. (00:43:43): I think that's where the intersection of the work between this... especially for a tech company, the CEO, CPO have to be... And even the CTO I would throw in the mix. That has to be very clearly articulated, otherwise it creates a lot of confusion. Those are some of the things, at least that I observe from different patterns and different companies that I've worked with and also guided and advised, those are things that always come up.
turns.zh:
是啊。我觉得这确实是个很有意思的话题。说真的，以我的经验来看，首席产品官（CPO）到底负责什么？他们的职责到底是什么？这值得好好探讨一下。一般来说，虽然每个公司各不相同，但我们可以先从共性角度来思考。总的来说，CPO需要为公司制定产品愿景，而这个产品愿景又必须与公司愿景紧密相连。这往往是领导团队内部产生冲突的根源——人们会提出宏伟的计划，比如“我们要做这个，要做那个”，但这些计划往往脱离了公司的实际情况。（00:41:09）  
CPO的第二大职责是执行产品路线图上的优先事项。有些人以为，到了高管层级就不用操心执行问题了。绝对不是这样！特别是CPO，即便CTO和工程部门负责人，执行能力也至关重要。面对复杂的运营环境，比如远程办公、各种工具套件、层出不穷的技术创新、激烈的竞争环境，执行力至关重要。如果高管们误以为升到高层后就不用关注执行问题，那他们就大错特错了。执行力是核心职责之一。  
（00:41:50）  
第三点，对于科技公司来说，CPO尤其重要，因为他们主导产品路线图，这是一个影响深远的角色。这意味着要与其他部门紧密合作，比如市场营销、销售、业务部门等，确保产品路线图真正贴合实际需求。可以说，CPO的工作是跨职能的、强化版的。  
（00:42:19）  
关于CEO和CPO的关系，我认为关键在于……这也是我给一些公司CEO的建议，尤其是在他们寻找产品副总裁或CPO时。我会给他们一份问卷。首先问CEO：你想做什么？这是最重要的问题。很多CEO要么是技术创始人，要么是产品创始人，甚至是销售创始人，这些都没问题。但你真正想花时间在哪方面？如果你招了CPO或产品副总裁后，自己还想掌控产品路线图和执行，那就别这么做了。因为这样的人能做什么？这就是我与寻求CPO或产品副总裁的CEO们首先要厘清的问题。  
（00:43:10）  
另外，要思考你是在优化流程？优化战略？还是优化团队建设和人才吸引？这很关键。有时你需要合适的领导层来吸引更多人才。比如人们会说：“哦，这个人在那家公司工作，我也要去他们公司。”你如何看待工程、数据科学和设计？如何看待GM和运营？这些都是需要深思熟虑的方面。
接下来，在决定是否聘请产品副总裁或首席产品官，以及希望招募怎样的候选人之前，你需要从设计角度考虑的关键要素。（00:43:43）：我认为这正是两者工作交集的核心领域……尤其对于科技公司而言，首席执行官和首席产品官必须……甚至首席技术官也应纳入考量范畴。这些职责必须清晰界定，否则会引发诸多混淆。这些都是我从不同模式、不同公司中观察到的共性问题，既有亲身经历，也有指导和咨询过的案例，这些问题始终反复出现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting how much similarity there is to that experience as there is to the first PM at a company. It feels like they have to have the same conversations with the founder. What do you want to work on? What am I going to take on? How do we avoid stepping on each other's toes the whole time?
turns.zh: 很有趣的是，这种经历和在公司担任首位产品经理的经历有诸多相似之处。感觉他们都得和创始人进行类似的对话。比如：你想着重发展哪些方面？我该承担哪些职责？我们怎样才能避免职责重叠？

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: That's actually a... I never thought about it that way, Lenny. I think that's a really good point. You're totally right. Obviously, if you're at a bigger company, then you're looking for a VP of product. Or if you're a super big company, then you're looking for a CPO. But you're right. The first product hire that you make as a founder, you'll pretty much have the same conversations to ensure that there are clear swim lanes and accountability for that group.
turns.zh: 这确实是个……我从没这么想过，莱尼。我觉得你说得太对了。显然，如果你在大公司任职，那你要找的是产品副总裁；要是超级大公司，那就得找首席产品官了。但你说得没错。作为创始人，你招聘的首位产品经理，几乎都会进行类似的对话，以确保团队职责分明、责任明确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. I want to make sure to ask you, as kind of a big deal leader of product at larger companies, I'm curious, what do you look for in PMs that are looking to get promoted, or just deciding somebody's ready for promotion or ready for more responsibility? What do you look for and what should people focus on if they want to come across as promotion material?
turns.zh: 有意思。我想问问你，作为大公司产品部门的重要负责人，对于那些渴望晋升、或者被认为已具备晋升资格、需要承担更多职责的产品经理，你会看重哪些方面？你会关注哪些品质？如果有人想成为晋升的候选人，又该重点培养哪些能力？

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: I'm a big fan of looking at both the what and the how. So what did they accomplish and how did they accomplish. Because they're a package. And if you just look at one versus the other, then I think you end up making a mistake. Usually. On the what, I think the what is usually more objective. What I look for... And again, it depends on the level of the person. Don't try to calibrate someone based early in their career. You have to think through that. That they're in learning phase. If they're more senior than you have to of course calibrate them differently. But ultimately, if I were to boil it down on the what, it's really about real demonstrated impact. An ideal example is someone who had a strong product hypothesis, they rallied a bunch of people around them. They may not have come up with the hypothesis. That's fine. Somebody else could have come up with it, it doesn't matter. But they believed in it, they rallied the team behind it, they drove towards it and created impact. (00:45:58): The impact not necessarily always has to be positive. It could also be a lot of stuff that we learned, but we learned from it and then we moved on and we did the next rev. By the time we did the next rev, we were smarter about it. Clear demonstrated impact from an end to end product cycle to me is probably one of the better indicators of readiness for someone to take on more. And you basically want to give them more, because now they have a pattern of doing things properly. That's one. (00:46:23): On the how, I just love people who are able to create both energy and create clarity. Think of the flip side. PMs who don't create clarity is such a time sink and the teams struggle so much. I'm sure all of us, when we think about back in the day, maybe we were in that position at some point. But we also worked with folks who were always confused and didn't really summarize, or didn't really follow up, or didn't really create that level of clarity in terms of what we need to do and so on, and how broken that felt. People who can create the clarity and then have the energy around them to get things done, I think that's the how in my opinion. Which is really important for determining somebody's career trajectory. (00:47:11): Then the last thing I would say is followership. Really important for PMs. Do people want to work with them? Do people at some point, as they go up and become more senior, do people want to work for them? Ultimately people make choices. And if you have a bunch of smart people and they're making smart choices and they're choosing this person to follow or to be with and work with them and reach out to them, and you keep hearing things about, hey, so and so wants to work with this person because this person is amazing; there is a ton of value in that. (00:47:45): Those are the three things that, if I were to really boil it down, not looking at a certain level, I think I always look for those attributes.
turns.zh: 我非常重视同时关注「结果」和「过程」。也就是说，他们取得了哪些成果，又是如何达成这些成果的。因为这两者是相辅相成的。如果你只关注其中一方面，我认为最终会犯错。这通常适用于评估成果部分。我认为成果评估通常更客观。我的衡量标准……这取决于对方的职级。不要在他们职业生涯早期就试图对他们进行评判。你必须考虑到他们处于学习阶段。如果他们比你资深，那当然需要用不同的标准来衡量。但归根结底，如果我要总结成果评估的核心，那就是真实的示范性影响力。理想的例子是某人提出了强有力的产品假设，成功召集团队支持它。假设这个假设不是他们原创的，这没关系。可能别人先提出的，但他们深信其正确性，团结团队朝着目标前进并创造了实际影响。（00:45:58）：影响力不一定总是正面的。也可能是我们从中吸取了教训，但吸取教训后继续前进，进行下一次迭代。到下一次迭代时，我们会更明智。对我来说，从端到端的产品周期中清晰展现出的影响力，或许是判断一个人是否能承担更多责任的最佳指标之一。因为现在他们已经形成了正确做事的模式。这是第一点。（00:46:23）：关于过程评估，我特别欣赏那些既能激发团队活力又能理清思路的人。想想相反的情况吧。那些无法理清思路的产品经理真是浪费时间，导致团队效率低下。相信我们所有人，回想过去，都曾遇到过类似情况。但我们也合作过那些总是困惑不已、无法总结任务、无法跟进、无法清晰传达工作重点的人，那种糟糕的感觉令人难忘。那些能理清思路并激发团队活力的人，在我看来这就是过程评估的精髓。这对判断一个人的职业发展轨迹至关重要。（00:47:11）：最后我想说的是追随力。对产品经理来说这非常重要。人们是否愿意与他们共事？当他们晋升到更高职级后，人们是否愿意为他们工作？归根结底，人都是会做出选择的。如果你身边有很多聪明的人，他们都在做出明智选择，选择追随这个人，与其共事、向其寻求帮助，并且不断听到「某某想和这个人合作，因为这个人太棒了」之类的评价，这其中的价值是巨大的。（00:47:45）：如果不考虑具体职级层级，这些就是我一直寻找的三个核心特质。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Those are awesome. So simple and clear and succinct. I like the way that you framed it as followership versus leadership. There's a lot of PM attributes leadership, and there's something really nice about just a way to understand that as how many people are following you and excited to work on the things that you're trying to get them to work on. That's very cool. (00:48:11): Along the same lines, when you think about PMs that had an inflection point in their career, do you find that there's anything correlated with something that leads to a large inflection in the progress of someone's career where they all of a sudden started doing incredibly better?
turns.zh: 这些观点太棒了。如此简洁明了、一针见血。我很欣赏你将领导力与追随力进行对比的视角。许多人将项目管理归功于领导力，而你这种用“有多少人追随你并乐于参与你设定的任务”来理解领导力的方式，实在妙不可言。太棒了。（00:48:11）：顺着这个思路，当我们谈及职业生涯中迎来转折点的项目经理时，你是否发现某些因素与职业发展中的重大突破相关联？比如他们突然间表现出色得多？

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: I've gone through a few inflection points myself, and almost always they've happened because something in the organization changed, so I got a shot. There's always that luck factor, going back to the first question that we discussed. (00:48:37): But generally speaking, I think the inflection points happen in two places. One is when someone has really successfully changed the dynamic, or the trajectory rather, of a particular product. That's a huge inflection point. That doesn't happen very often, to be fair. But when it happens, you know it. You know, as a leader, this person worked on this and they actually led this change and now we are playing a different game. We are playing a bigger game, we are playing a different game, all of that kind of stuff. (00:49:16): In other words, what I'm saying is the inflection point for a career is correlated strongly with the inflection point in the product. If you can connect those, the cause and effect... If there's causality and not just correlation, if there's causality in that, I think that absolutely means that you've got a winner. And you really want to bet on them and you have to give them a lot more to do, because they have the ability to do it. That's one. (00:49:38): The second is, oftentimes as people go up in their career, they start managing teams. They become a manager, and then you become a manager of managers, and then you become more senior. I mean, that's the organizational trajectory that happens. One inflection point that I've seen is, when you go from being a manager, a first line manager, to becoming a manager of managers, and if you're able to navigate that with very strong effectiveness, then you know. If you're their manager or if you're their leader you know this person has got their act together. Because managing ICs is so different from managing managers, because then you now need to create a structure. You need to be able to determine how much you delegate. How do you coach? How do coach your managers to do the right thing? If you see somebody making that transition effectively... And you have to give them some time, but if you see that and you know that they're actually doing it, and again, a lot of followership, a lot of other things are happening, good things are happening, then you know they're at that inflection point where they're ready to take on more. (00:50:41): Both product inflection in terms of real output and this management prowess inflection in terms of being able to effectively lead going from one step to another, a manager to becoming a manager of managers; I think those are the two places where I feel like, if I see somebody doing well, I know they're ready to put more onto them.
turns.zh:
我自己也经历过几个转折点，几乎每一次都是因为组织内部发生了变化，我才获得了机会。这里又回到了我们讨论过的第一个问题，运气因素始终存在。（00:48:37）：但总的来说，我认为转折点主要出现在两个方面。第一，当某人成功改变了某个产品的动态或发展轨迹时，这就是一个重大的转折点。说实话，这种情况并不常见。但一旦发生，你就能感知到。作为领导者，你会意识到这个人参与了变革，现在我们在玩一场不同的游戏，参与更大规模的竞争，等等。（00:49:16）：换句话说，我想说的是，职业生涯的转折点与产品的转折点紧密相关。如果能将两者关联起来，形成因果关系而非简单相关性，那就意味着这个人注定会成功。必须全力支持他们，赋予他们更多责任，因为他们有能力胜任。第一点。
（00:49:38）：第二点是，随着职业晋升，人们往往开始管理团队。先是成为一线经理，接着成为管理者的管理者，再逐步晋升。我指的是组织层级的递进。我见过的一个转折点是，从一线管理者晋升为管理者的管理者。如果能高效应对这一转变，你就能察觉到不同。无论是管理个体贡献者，还是管理管理者，本质区别在于前者只需关注产出，而后者需要构建组织架构，合理分配权责，指导下属正确行事。如果看到有人成功完成这种转变——这需要给他们时间观察——但当你确认他们确实做到了，你就能确定他们已准备好迎接更重大的挑战。
（00:50:41）：无论是产品层面的产出突破，还是管理层面的能力提升——从管理者晋升为管理者的管理者——我认为这两个转折点至关重要。如果看到有人表现出色，我就能确定他们已做好准备，可以承受更多重任。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you find that second piece is this filter for PMs that do well in this manager manager role and go on to do better and better and then a lot just fall away because they can't handle that?
turns.zh: 你是否发现，那些在管理者角色中表现出色、不断进步的员工，往往会因为无法胜任后续工作而逐渐失去竞争力？

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: Yeah, I think so. Maybe I'm a little bit more traditionist on this point. I know there are other schools of thought on this, which I respect. Which is there are a lot of times where people are like, "Well, oftentimes the best PMs are PMs who are IC PMs. They have this crazy, incredible, unbounded energy and they don't want to waste their time on management and whatnot and do that. Because a large part of a PM's job, by the way, is managing by influence. PMs typically don't have large organizations. In fact, one of the most leveraged teams in almost every company... Because you talk about PM manage ratios, PM design ratios, they're never one-ish to one, or one-ish to five, or one-ish to six. Sometimes it' going to be one-ish to 10. At Google it used to be one-ish to eight to one-ish to 10. (00:51:52): I personally see that transition... If somebody's making that transition successfully and they're getting good scores out of it and delivering the product and the output of the team is significant, I definitely see that as a good filter criteria for someone whom we can bet on.
turns.zh: 是啊，我也这么认为。或许在这点上我更倾向于传统观点。我知道其他人对此有不同看法，我对此表示尊重。很多时候人们会说：“嗯，最优秀的产品经理往往是专注于产品管理的‘内部产品经理’。他们精力充沛、才华横溢，根本不想把时间浪费在管理琐事上。”毕竟，产品经理的工作很大一部分在于通过影响力进行管理。他们通常没有管理大团队的资源。事实上，几乎所有公司中最具影响力的团队……比如产品经理的管理比例、产品设计比例，从来都不是1比1，或者1比5、1比6，有时甚至是1比10。在谷歌，曾经是1比8到1比10。（00:51:52）就我个人而言，我认为这种转变……如果有人能成功完成这种转变，取得良好的成果，交付出色的产品，并且团队产出显著，那么我绝对会把这视为一个值得信赖的人才的筛选标准。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you find there's common habits or pitfalls PMs make to shoot themselves in the foot in their career, especially early on?
turns.zh: 你是否发现产品经理在职业生涯早期常会犯一些自毁前程的习惯或错误？

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: Oh, I see that all the time. There's a few of the things that I have picked up. And by the way, I was doing this too early on and I learned the hard way. The first one I would talk about is you are early in your career and everyone expects you to just manage things and manage the process and all of that. Make sure that trains are running on time and all of that. Which, by the way, is really important for an early in career PM to understand. That that's actually a big part of your job. Let's not over glamorize a PM. A large part of being a PM initially is just basically doing whatever the team needs you to do. But I think one of the pitfalls of that is, if you start putting process over progress, that's a problem. (00:52:58): What I mean by that is, you want to introduce process into almost everything that the team does and not be flexible on shipping things out there and all the things that can come in the way of progress. If process is helping progress, great. But if process is hurting progress, you should not be the person saying, "No, no, no, no. We can't do it, because I'm just so married to the process. Because as a PM, that's what I own." I mean, as a PM you don't write code typically, you don't write design specs, you write product specs. Sometimes you feel like, what is the set of attributes that I own? Especially early in career PMs. And you're like, "I own this process. I own this weekly standup meeting, or I own this sprint planning, or whatever." And then you get so married to it that you forget the fact that that's just a means to an end and the end is what you're going to be actually measured on. That's one mistake that I see people making early on. (00:53:48): The second one is becoming really too self-centered. It's all about me, not the team. I'm the PM. There's this myth that keeps going around. The PM is the CEO of the product. That's one of the most incorrect things in the world. The PM is an enabler. I said earlier, it's a leverage job. Your job is to really make the team successful. Of course you have to have the product thinking and the roadmap and all of that, but sometimes this can go to their head. Then people become too self-centered and that's a red flag. (00:54:21): Then the third one would be just not admitting your mistakes or learning from them. Early in career, the only thing you should optimize for is learning. Sure, you'll make a lot of mistakes. You don't know much yet. You're just coming into this journey and you should be humble and you should be learning and you should be saying, "Oops, I screwed up over here." And that's okay. That's fine. And by the way, if you work in a company where that is not accepted, you should not work in that company. What's the point? You should really be optimizing for learning and learning from other people. And people should be saying, "Yeah, don't worry. It's okay. You made the mistake. Learn from it. Don't make the mistake again. That's fine." But that's the kind of culture you want to choose for yourself. (00:55:01): Those are the three pitfalls that I see people get into, especially early on in their career.
turns.zh: 哦，我经常遇到这种情况。以下是我总结的一些经验之谈。顺便说一句，我早期在职场时也犯过类似错误，吃了不少苦头。首先要说的是，刚入行的新人往往被期望能处理各种事务，比如确保项目按时推进、协调流程等等。这确实是初级项目经理需要理解的重要职责。但要注意，如果过度重视流程而忽视进展，那就是个大问题了。（00:52:58）我的意思是，团队做任何事时你都要引入流程，但不能因此僵化进展流程。若流程能助力进展，那固然好。但若流程阻碍进展，你就不能死守条条框框说：“不行不行，我必须按流程来”，因为作为项目经理，你的职责是统筹全局。（00:53:48）第二个误区是过度以自我为中心。总觉得“我是项目经理，团队都是围着我转”。这种“产品CEO”的神话实在是误区。项目经理本质上是赋能者。我之前说过，这是一份杠杆作用的工作。你的职责是助力团队成功。当然你需要具备产品思维、路线图规划等能力，但有时会因此膨胀。（00:54:21）第三个问题是拒绝承认错误并从中学习。初期阶段，唯一该优化的是学习能力。难免会犯错，毕竟你经验不足。保持谦逊，善于总结：“哎呀，我这里做错了”。这完全没问题。顺便说一句，如果公司不包容这种心态，就别去那里工作。何必呢？你应该优先优化学习能力，多向他人请教。同事应该说：“没关系，犯错很正常。吸取教训，下次别再犯就行。” 这才是你应该选择的文化环境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You touched on how different companies work in different ways and look for different things in different PMs. And something I wanted to ask you is just to chat a bit about the difference between working at Google versus Uber versus Microsoft as a PM, and also just generally how product is built differently at these companies. It's something I'm trying to do with this podcast as much as possible. Just give an overview of what product is like at different companies. You've worked at three of the biggest, and so I'm curious to hear what you can share around that.
turns.zh: 你提到了不同公司的工作方式各不相同，对产品经理的要求也各有侧重。我想问问你，能否简单谈谈在谷歌、优步和微软担任产品经理的不同之处，以及这些公司构建产品的方式有何不同。这也是我通过这个播客尽可能想做到的一件事——概括不同公司产品部门的运作模式。你曾在三家行业巨头任职，我很期待听听你对此的见解。

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: Yeah. It's actually really interesting. I mean, all the three companies are so different. Google, the core DNA of the company was very much engineering. In fact, there used to be a framework which was around technology insights drive innovation. It was always about what is the best tech we can come up with, which is going to indeed drive innovation, and have a longish view so that the market will get there. That was the Google philosophy always. As a PM, your job at Google... It might have changed in the last six, seven years that I've not been there, but at least when I was there from 2008 to 2015, especially working on Google Maps, it was all about how do you take good long-term bets grounded in strong technical insights, and then use the power of Google Search distribution to really get your product out there. That was it. (00:56:33): On the Maps team, our innovation was pretty much around crowdsourcing everyone's location signals for traffic. Huge, huge accomplishment. We had the best traffic models in the world. And then being able to do this crazy route optimization for driving directions. Then on top of that, we had the search stack, which came from Google Search anyway. So that you can search for any address, any business and so on. (00:56:55): Anyway, as a PM it was partnering very closely with engineers and really amplifying the engineer's ideas and so on. I think at that point also a lot of Google PMs were very technical. Very, very technical. Because that was just part for the course. It was expected that you will be able to at least have engineering discussions. A large part of what I did as a PM at Google, especially initially, was getting into the technical details with my engineers and really geeking out on what we can do. That was the Google model. (00:57:25): By the way, one thing I should say about Google before I go to... At Google as a PM, at least all the way up to the time even when I became a director, I never had to think about business models, man. Never. It was fascinating. You were in this weird state where you could just build and have the consumer traction and all of that, but you never thought about P&L, never thought about revenue and so on. (00:57:48): Then I landed at Uber, which was very different. Uber was very operations, very business driven, very P&L. In fact, one of the most incredible things that Uber did was they had a dashboard which every employee in the company could look at, and it had last week's revenue, last week's number of trips that we did, and you could slice and dice it and all of that. I think that changed over time as we became a public company and so on. But the point was that it was really in your face all the time. When there were weekly newsletters sent out, it was all about growth, it was all about business, all of that kind of stuff. It was very operational and business, so as a PM over there it was a lot about managing a bunch more stakeholders. The operations teams, the marketing teams, the policy teams and so on. And how do you work with them to deploy your product into each of these markets. Of course then a large chunk of your work was still working with the engineering team. It was different in that sense. (00:58:47): I think at Uber the other thing was it was also much more of a real time business. I mean, Google was also real time. Google Maps was real time. Billions of users were using it. But Uber was... every day there was something going on in the market and you had to keep on that hustle in terms of how do you make sure that your staying competitive, your product is working well, there are no outages. All of that kind of stuff was really important. (00:59:09): Then finally, on Microsoft... I mean, Microsoft has been around for quite a while. The company went through so many different things and then over the last several years, especially under Satya's leadership, it has done so well. Incredibly well in terms of how the company has changed the culture, the kind of products that they have in the market, the traction they have in the market. (00:59:29): I think I would describe Microsoft as both... first and foremost, it's a very strong tech company. The engineers here are incredible. Oh my God. I am so privileged to work with some of the best engineers that I've worked with in my career. At the same time there's a lot of legacy. There are a lot of products that have been around for a really long time, which is good and bad. The good part is that they have seen pretty much every pattern there is to see. In fact, they came up with a lot of those patterns themselves. The bad part sometimes can be that change is hard. How do you convince people that we're going to go down a different path? As a PM, a lot of it is around bringing outside in perspective, bringing clarity of like, "Hey, this is how it has actually worked somewhere else." Bring a specific example. Let's try it out and see how that works. (01:00:13): The final thing I would say about it is the company is so grounded in trust. If there's one word that I would say about Microsoft is trust. They really care a lot about customers. Customers trust Microsoft a lot. I've been in some of the customer meetings myself and I can totally hear what customers say. It's all about trust. They expect resilience, they expect the products to work, and they expect that when they have a problem on the surface, that Microsoft will take care of it. They built that over time. A lot of that goes into your mind as a PM when you're working in that company, that a lot of the stuff that we are doing here is to really help our customers.
turns.zh:
是啊。这其实非常有趣。我想，这三家公司都截然不同。谷歌的核心DNA一直深深植根于工程技术。事实上，过去曾有一个框架，强调技术洞察力驱动创新。核心在于，我们要开发出最佳的技术方案，推动创新，并着眼于长远视野，让市场最终跟上步伐。这始终是谷歌的理念。作为产品经理，在谷歌工作……虽然过去六七年我没待在那里，但至少2008年至2015年我在那里的时候，尤其是参与谷歌地图项目时，关键在于如何基于强有力的技术洞察力，做出长期优质的赌注，然后借助谷歌搜索的分发力量，将产品推向市场。就是这样。（00:56:33）：在地图团队，我们的创新主要围绕众包收集用户位置数据用于交通导航。这是巨大的成就。我们拥有全球最先进的交通模型，还能实现疯狂的路线优化算法。此外，我们还能利用源自谷歌搜索的搜索引擎栈，用户可以搜索任何地址、商家等。（00:56:55）：总之，作为产品经理，需要与工程师密切合作，放大他们的创意。我记得那时很多谷歌产品经理都非常技术型，极其精通技术，因为这就是必备的技能。作为产品经理，我的工作重点之一就是与工程师深入探讨技术细节，尽情钻研可能性。这就是谷歌模式。（00:57:25）：顺便说一句，关于谷歌……至少在我担任产品经理直至成为总监期间，谷歌从不强制我们考虑商业模式。完全不需要操心。这很奇妙。你处于一种奇特的状态，可以专注于产品开发，享受用户增长的红利，却无需操心利润表、收入等事务。（00:57:48）：后来我加入优步，情况完全不同。优步高度重视运营，商业导向明显，利润表至上。事实上，优步最令人惊叹的创新之一是推出仪表板，全公司员工都能查看上周的收入、订单量等数据，还能进行多维度分析。随着优步上市，这种数据透明化程度逐渐降低。但关键在于，商业压力始终如影随形。每周的周报都聚焦于增长、商业策略等核心议题。这里更偏向于运营和商业层面，作为产品经理，需要协调更多利益相关方——运营团队、市场团队、政策团队等，确保产品在各个市场顺利落地。当然，核心工作仍是与工程团队紧密合作。两者的差异显著。（00:58:47）：我认为优步的另一个特点是实时商业模式。谷歌同样具备实时性，但谷歌地图是面向数十亿用户的服务。优步则每天都要应对市场动态，必须持续保持竞争力。
产品运行良好，没有出现故障。所有这些方面都非常重要。（00:59:09）：最后，说到微软……我的意思是，微软已经存在很久了。这家公司经历了诸多变革，尤其是在过去几年里，在萨蒂亚的领导下，它发展得非常出色。无论是公司文化的变革、市场上的产品阵容，还是产品的市场影响力，都令人惊叹。（00:59:29）：我认为微软既……首先，它是一家非常强大的科技公司。这里的工程师非常出色。天哪，能与职业生涯中最优秀的工程师共事，我深感荣幸。同时，微软也有很多传统遗产。许多产品已经存在很久了，这既有利也有弊。好处是他们几乎见证了所有可能出现的模式，甚至很多模式都是他们自己开创的。坏处在于变革往往困难重重。比如，要说服人们接受新的发展方向，作为产品经理，关键在于引入外部视角，清晰传达：“看，这在其他地方是如何成功的。” 用具体案例来说明，尝试后再验证效果。（01:00:13）：最后，微软非常注重信任。如果用一个词来形容微软，那就是“信任”。他们非常关心客户，客户也非常信任微软。我亲自参加过一些客户会议，完全能感受到客户的需求。一切都围绕信任展开。他们期望产品具备高可靠性，期望产品正常运行，期望出现表面问题时微软能及时解决。这种信任是他们长期积累的。作为产品经理，在微软工作时，你会深切体会到，我们所做的一切都是为了更好地服务客户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Going back to your point about company-product fit, these cultures and the way they work just fits perfectly with the thing they end up building. I wonder which one comes first.
turns.zh: 回到你关于公司与产品契合度的观点，这些文化以及它们的运作方式与最终开发的产品完美契合。我很好奇哪个先行一步。

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: It's true. That's a whole nother conversation we can have at some point. I have a lot of thoughts on that. But I'll just echo what you just said, which is that's the reason why it's so important for companies, when they embark on new initiatives, to be really, really thoughtful. Is this the right area for us to get into? Or rather, what are the conditions and the reasons why we are getting into something? We have to be super clear on that. Because if the starting conditions are not right, then you will just trash the team. The team will keep working on something and people will never find the right internal fit. So that's super important.
turns.zh: 确实如此。这是我们可以深入探讨的另一个话题。我对此有很多想法。但我只想回应你刚才说的，这就是为什么公司在开展新项目时，必须要非常、非常谨慎的原因。这是我们要涉足的正确领域吗？或者说，我们涉足某个领域的条件和原因是什么？我们必须对此有非常清晰的认识。因为如果初始条件不正确，那么你就会毁掉整个团队。团队会继续在某件事上努力，但人们永远找不到内部契合的点。所以这非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You worked on Google Maps and Uber, which I imagine you still use often and maybe billions of people use every day. Is there a feature that you wish that you built back when you were on the team, or that you think should be killed, that annoys you about either of those products?
turns.zh: 你曾参与谷歌地图和优步的开发，我想你现在可能还经常使用它们，或许每天都有数十亿人使用。是否有你希望在团队时就开发的功能，或者认为应该被取消的功能，让你对其中任何一款产品感到厌烦？

turns.speaker: Manik Gupta
turns.en: Wow. Okay. This is a super interesting one. I don't know if that's something that I could have built at Google Maps, but one of the things that's interesting is the self-driving technology has just not gotten there fast enough. I feel like the best and brightest actually worked on it and are still working on it and it will get there. I'm a big believer. But of course the timelines have shifted for various reasons, because it is a really hard problem. It's actually really interesting to see what Cruise is doing right now in SF. They have started the pilots and so on, so I'm really happy to see some progress happening. I know Waymo's been doing a bunch of this already. (01:02:29): But it would've been amazing. One of the things that we used to talk about all the time at Google on Maps was how would we design a navigation product when people are in self-driving cars? We had some really interesting ideas at that point, but we never got to it. Not because we didn't prioritize it, but the technology isn't there. I still keep a close watch on that and see at what point are we going to get there. It's going to take years, but it is just such a different paradigm. It's like computers talking to computers, algorithms talking to other algorithms. Then there's a human in the mix in terms of serving the human at the end, but it's like the human is not initiating that much. It's just, stuff is happening around it. (01:03:08): Anyway, that's one thing that is unfinished business, if you will, in my mind. And hopefully, as the technology comes together, that will happen.
